In the “real world” of minor keys, things are sometimes more complicated. For instance, the v chord is often converted to a major triad or dominant seventh chord (Fig. 6), so as to contain the /eading tone. The leading tone is the major 7th scale degree, which in turn jeads upward by a half step to the tonic, creating a powerful sense of resolution. The major scale already contains the leading tone of course, but the 7th degree of the minor scale is a whole step below the tonic, making the pull to

resolution much less dramatic, 4) Fig. 6

TRACK 28

The V7 chord in minor keys can lead to confusion, because the >VIJ chord is also dominant in quality. But there is still a “dead giveaway” chord in minor keys: the m7>5, which functions as the ii chord. Also, half-step root movement, from the bVI to the V (and vice versa} is a common occurrence in minor keys.
